name: Penobscot
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Voorhis, Paul H. 1979. Grammatical Notes on the Penobscot Language from Frank Speck's Penobscot Transformer Tales. Winnipeg: Department of Anthropology, University of Manitoba. 83 pp. Open PDF, University of Manitoba MSpace, hdl 1993/18305.
catalog_locator: p. 12, section 2 Phonology, accent paragraph; also p. 11 on Speck's acute/grave marks and pp. 64-65 noun/verb stem list. rendered.
catalog_quote: There is frequent variation in the place of accent; the few discernable patterns are subject to many exceptions: élǝmihlvt 'he going along' (E.184) elǝmíhlvt 'he going along' (E.143) nǝkawáci 'I am cold' (9.39) káwaco 'it (for 'he'?) was cold' (9.26) ... Many stems seem to have a basic accent on a certain syllable, and the accent tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion: awás 'beast' (2.27) awássvk 'animals' (2.18) awássǝtok 'animals' (vocative) (2.16) ... nolítǝhasi 'I am glad' (E.58) wǝlítǝhyso 'she rejoiced' (E.107) étociwǝlítǝhasit 'she feeling so glad' (E.216) Certain suffixes, however, cause the accent to change; for example, in noun inflexion, the accent often shifts to the syllable preceding -m-, -ǝnaw-, and -owy-, see below.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Eastern Abenaki (Penobscot) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Siebert 1988 'The suprasegmental phonemes of the Penobscot dialect of Eastern Abenaki' (In Honor of Mary Haas, 715-764, DOI 10.1515/9783110852387.715), is the the deciding source but remains paywalled (De Gruyter; archive.org copy lending-restricted could not be reached by automated download text; not in HathiTrust/Google Books) — priority high; Harvard the Harvard library catalogue has online access per our check. Read in this search of works with stress in the title: Voorhis 1979 (open PDF found on University of Manitoba MSpace, hdl 1993/18305, previously marked print-only) gives the only first-hand accent statement — accent is a phoneme with 'frequent variation in the place of accent', lexically fixed on many noun stems and shifted by certain suffixes; verb-stem accents 'too uncertain to be indicated' (pp. 12, 64-65). Open Algonquian Conference papers add second-hand pieces of Siebert's system: Quinn 1999:291 relays Siebert 1988:729 (in open penultimate syllables all vowels except schwa lengthen to four moras); Siebert 1988 Tag-questions describes three phrase-level intonation prosodemes and tonic/atonic primary accent; Quinn 2001 notes high vs. low accent and that accent normally falls within the last few syllables. Speck 1918 marks stress but states no rule; Rasles 1833 and O'Brien 1887 (Norridgewock dialect) give nothing. Not obtained: Quinn 2006 Harvard dissertation (ProQuest only), Quinn's 'Reader Guide to the Penobscot Language' in Still They Remember Me (2021, JSTOR/MUSE, pp. 47-52; likely a plain statement of the accent marks), Siebert's unpublished dictionary introduction, Goddard 1978 (HNAI 15).org, Open Library, OJS, MSpace and Wikipedia APIs.

new_statements.quote: There is frequent variation in the place of accent; the few discernable patterns are subject to many exceptions: [...] Many stems seem to have a basic accent on a certain syllable, and the accent tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion: awás 'beast' (2.27) awássvk 'animals' (2.18) awássətok 'animals' (vocative) (2.16) [...] Certain suffixes, however, cause the accent to change; for example, in noun inflexion, the accent often shifts to the syllable preceding -m-, -ənaw-, and -owy-, see below.
new_statements.citation: Voorhis, Paul H. 1979. Grammatical Notes on the Penobscot Language from Frank Speck's Penobscot Transformer Tales. Winnipeg: Department of Anthropology, University of Manitoba.
new_statements.locator: p. 12 (p. 15); see also p. 11 (p. 14) and pp. 64-65 (pp. 67-68), section 2 Phonology / noun-stem list
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (86 pp., Canon scan; scanned layer garbled) and rendered pp. 14-15 and 67-68 (printed pp. 11-12, 64-65) to page scan. Printed p. 12 (p. 15) reads exactly: "There is frequent variation in the place of accent; the few discernable patterns are subject to many exceptions:" [six examples incl. élǝmihlvt (E.184) ~ elǝmíhlvt (E.143)] "Many stems seem to have a basic accent on a certain syllable, and the accent tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion:" [awás 'beast' (2.27), awássvk 'animals' (2.18), awássǝtok 'animals' (vocative) (2.16)..] "Certain suffixes, however, cause the accent to change; for example, in noun inflexion, the accent often shifts to the syllable preceding -m…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Voorhis (from Speck's transcriptions): no positional rule is discernible; each noun stem carries a lexically fixed 'basic accent' on a particular syllable that generally survives inflection, with some suffixes attracting the accent to the syllable before them. Second-hand indications of the authoritative analysis (Siebert 1988, unread): a tonic/atonic primary-accent system with open-penult vowel lengthening (all vowels except schwa lengthened in open penultimate syllables; Quinn 1999:291 citing Siebert 1988:729) and a 'usual pattern' bounded near the right edge (Quinn 2001 fn. 29, 31), so the catalog reading may need revision to a weight/penult-based rule once Siebert 1988 is read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Speck 1918 phonetic key marks primary and secondary stress; Voorhis merges Speck's acute (first/only accent) and grave (all other accents) into a single accent phoneme as complementarily distributed (p. 11). Nothing further on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent placement varies frequently between tokens of the same stem (e.g. élemihlvt ~ elemíhlvt 'he going along'); certain suffixes shift the accent (in noun inflection to the syllable before -m-, -enaw-, -owy-); verb-stem accents 'if there are any, are too uncertain to be indicated' (pp. 64-65).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in Speck's 1918 text transcriptions (running text, not elicited citation forms); Voorhis analyses Speck's marks, not his own recordings. Siebert's later phonemic work treats primary accent as tonic vs atonic 'suprasegmentals of primary accent' with a separate phrase-level intonation layer (Siebert 1988 Tag-questions, pp. 187-188).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Penobscot dialect of Eastern Abenaki (Indian Island, Maine), which Glottolog subsumes under east2544 (no separate dialect glottocode listed in the target record). Rasles 1833 and O'Brien 1887 concern the extinct Norridgewock (Caniba) dialect of Eastern Abenaki, not Penobscot. Western Abenaki (west2630) is a different language and was not used.

tone_statements.quote: The Penobscots accentuate their words in much the same manner as do their distant neighbors the Passamaquoddies ; i. e., they sing their syllables, giving sometimes to the first and often to the second, third, and fourth syllable of a combination, a rising inflection and then allowing the voice to fall on the succeeding syllable. ... This difficult system of tones can be learned only by practice, as there is apparently no rule for the place of the variable rising inflection. The Abenaki intonation, on the other hand, is very monotonous, as every syllable has practically the same accented value.

sources.quote: Further complicating the matter is that the morphemes involving schwa and h often occur in the penultimate syllable; as Siebert (1988:729) has explained, in open penultimate syllables all Penobscot vowels except schwa are lengthened to four moras. [...] An exception to the general pattern of open-penultimate vowel lengthening is precisely when the vowel precedes h. This exception is not mentioned in his article on Penobscot suprasegmentals (Siebert 1988), but Siebert told me so on one occasion
sources.note: p. 291, second-hand from Siebert 1988:729: 'in open penultimate syllables all Penobscot vowels except schwa are lengthened to four moras'; exception before h (Siebert p.c.); schwa 'never lengthens in the penult'. No explicit accent-placement rule quoted.

sources.citation: Siebert, Frank T. (1988). Tag-questions in Penobscot. Papers of the Algonquian Conference 19: 187-190.
sources.quote: In the Penobscot dialect of Eastern Abenaki ordinary interrogation is indicated by one of the three suprasegmental phonemes of intonation (or prosodemes) whose domain is the phrase. [...] Also, the interrogative prosodeme is often associated with mutations of the accompanying suprasegmentals of primary accent, changing them from atonic to tonic. All the details of ordinary interrogation are described in full elsewhere (Siebert 1988).
sources.note: Sentence intonation: three phrase-level intonation prosodemes; interrogative intonation raises the final syllable a major second to major third and is 'often associated with mutations of the accompanying suprasegmentals of primary accent, changing them from atonic to tonic'; defers word accent details to Siebert 1988 (Haas volume).

sources.note: Pp. 19-21 describe Penobscot word 'intonation' as a 'difficult system of tones': a rising inflection (marked with acute) on a variable syllable (1st-4th), a voice-drop (grave) on the next syllable, and often a lower secondary rise (inverted circumflex) on a following final syllable; 'there is apparently no rule for the place of the variable rising inflection'; St. Francis Abenaki by contrast is 'very monotonous', every syllable with the same accented value; Prince regards the Penobscot (and Passamaquoddy) system as the original one.
